utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-03-69-T. The Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before the next witness will be called, a few matters. The Stanisic Defence has in addition to the reason given earlier for the accused to be provisionally released added to that they would like to be authorised to visit his father's grave. Mr. Groome, is there any -- do you want to respond to that, if so, would you like to do it now or will I set a dead-line for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, on that specific matter if the Chamber does grant provisional release the Prosecution will have no objection to him visiting his father's grave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. The Stanisic Defence has requested leave to reply to the Prosecution's response. Any objection against this request?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the Stanisic Defence request for leave to reply is granted hereby. Mr. Jordash, I think it would be in the interest of the Stanisic Defence that we receive that reply as soon as possible. We are even thinking about today but that might be too early. Tomorrow midday, would that ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I just consult, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Today, Your Honour, would be fine with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you could manage, multitasking is that called, is it? Yes, you would like to leave the reply, I was thinking about a written reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So were we, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, you were on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I wanted to add a few words to this. I wanted to ask for leave, oral leave from the Trial Chamber that we also file a response to the Prosecution's reply and we would do that by late tonight. However, I think it's unrealistic that to expect that we can file it by tonight, but we would manage to do so during the course of the morning if we are granted leave to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Prosecution would not object to leave being granted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Bakrac, leave is granted, we expect you to file it tomorrow in the course of the morning until midday. If perhaps already before filing tomorrow morning you would have a courtesy copy available to the Chamber, that would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then last matter I put on the record that the Chamber informed the parties on the 3rd of December, although relatively late, at 7.00 p.m., that it had decided, and it was based on some discussions in court and apparently discussions between the parties after court time, that the testimony of Ewa Tabeau would commence on Tuesday the 7th of December, as was then scheduled. That the testimony of witness of JF-029 will not commence before Wednesday, the 8th of December, and that in the event that the testimony of Ewa Tabeau does not conclude by the end of Tuesday, the 7th of December, that the Chamber will consider whether to interrupt the testimony of Ms. Tabeau in order to commence with witness JF-029. We'll -- when making such a determination, we'll of course carefully consider all of the circumstances. This is hereby put on the record. I have no further matters to be raised at this moment. Is the Prosecution ready to call Ms. Tabeau?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I should apologise, I should perhaps have jumped to my feet earlier. It's -- may I address Your Honour, an issue concerning this next witness's testimony concerning 14 additional victims that have been the subject of an application to add to the exhibit list, dated the 1st of October 2010 as part of the Prosecution's submission of the updated victim's support of expert witness Tabeau and motion to add proof of death documents to Rule 65 ter exhibit list. We've been informed by the Prosecution that to the extent the indictment or schedule attached thereto expressly mentioned additional unnamed victims, those additional victims, the 14, are, according to the Prosecution, to be added to the indictment. This particular witness mentions those 14 and perhaps what I'm requesting is that we be allowed to address you on whether those 14 are allowed to be added to the indictment in the way that the Prosecution are proposing, which is to basically do it without asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's -- I suggest that we start hearing the evidence of Ms. Tabeau and at the last five minutes before the break, because I find it not very appropriate to let her wait outside, otherwise if you would have asked before --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, it's my fault entirely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, may the witness be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that what, at least, I expect will be the contents of the testimony, that it will not really become a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: There will be no prejudice by dealing with it this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Tabeau. Before you give evidence, you are required to make a solemn declaration, the text of is it handed out to you, may I invite you to make a solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Tabeau. Please be seated. Ms. Tabeau, you'll first be examined by Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Tabeau. Can you hear me clearly?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Could you please state your full name for the record?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Ewa Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, I note that you've brought some papers with you to court today, can you please tell the Chamber what those papers are?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: One binder contains the text of my reports, and some additional documents like my professional qualifications, like some presentations prepared for this testimony, some sources that were used for this project. The other two binders contain excerpts or full proof of the documents that were compiled for this project.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask the Chamber's leave that Dr. Tabeau be permitted to consult her reports and the other materials in the course of her testimony as required. These are all materials that have been disclosed to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Leave is granted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, your professional qualifications are outlined on page 108 of your IDP's and refugees report which is 65 ter number 5864, and in your CV which has been uploaded as 65 ter number 5867, so I won't go over your background in detail. I do have a few clarification questions, though. Your CV indicates that you received your PhD in mathematical demography in 1991. What was the focus of your research for your PhD?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I studied differences in mortality in Poland, regional differences and factors underlying these differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your CV also indicates that you were a senior researcher and project leader at the Dutch Interdisciplinary Demographic Institute from 1991 to 2000? What was the focus of your work there?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: My research area was the study of mortality in western countries and central European countries. I studied mortality, overall mortality, mortality by cause of death, life expectancy, prospects for longevity, this was a study meant to, first of all, focus mortality, overall or by cause of death, and secondly, to explain the differences in mortality for various social groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Since 2000, you have been employed by the Office of the Prosecution here at the ICTY. Your CV indicates that during that time you've prepared approximately 40 expert reports. In how many of those reports have you used a methodology similar to the methodology you used for your reports in this case?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The methodology used for this report, for this case is a standard methodology used by the demographic unit of the Office of the Prosecution, so basically the answer would be practically in all other reports, the same methodology was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: As far as you know, were these reports admitted as expert reports in the cases in which they were presented?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, yes, of course, these were reports presented as expert reports and tendered, majority of them into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr, would that not be something that you could have agreed upon? I mean, let's try to get to the core, and of course, I'm very happy to know exactly what the focus of Ms. Tabeau's work was in the past, but I'm primarily interested at this moment in the report. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I'll proceed, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, during your testimony here today we'll be dealing with two reports you prepared specifically for this case. The full title of the first report is: "Ethnic Composition, Internally Displaced Persons and Refugees from Five Municipalities of Bosnia and Herzegovina, 1991 to 1997/1998." The updated version that we will be using in this case is dated 9 July 2010. The previous version was first filed on 15 December 2004 and that report has 65 ter 5864. I will refer to that report as "the IDP's and refugees report" in the rest of my examination.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct, this is the first report.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: The full title of the second report is: "Victims of War Related to the Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic Indictment." It is dated 6 August 2010 with the exception of annex 4 to that report which is dated 23 September 2010. That report is 65 ter 5748 and I will refer to that report as "the victims report."

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, that's the second report.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: During your testimony today we'll discuss the sources, methodology and results for each report. We'll deal with the IDP's and refugees report first. In that report, you identify the 1991 population census. And the 1997/1998 voters' registers as the two principal sources and describe them at pages 5 to 9 in annex B. My question is: Can you comment briefly on the size and completeness of those two sources as compared to sources commonly used in demographic or statistical studies?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The population census is the most complete population survey existing so in principal it is meant to cover the entire population, and basically did cover the entire population of Bosnia and Herzegovina as of March -- end of March 1991. The size of the population census for Bosnia is 4.4 million individual records and we did use the individual micro-level information about persons and not aggregate statistics, so it is the most existing, most complete record of information about a population, the population in a country. The voters' register is not as large as the population census, it is, basically speaking, a large sample of the population eligible to vote, that is those who at the time of elections were 18 or older, 18 years or older, and it covers those eligible voters who registered to vote. But still its size was large for Bosnia and Herzegovina; it covered approximately 2.5 million individuals. Merged voters' register 1997 and 1998 covered altogether 2.7 million individuals and again we used individual-level records from the voters' registration. So these sources are exceptionally large and exceptionally broad. In statistics and demography, sample surveys are often used which are very small and of course even though they are representative, they cannot compare with sources like the population census or the voters' register.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And what is the impact on the reliability of your results of having sources that are exceptionally large and exceptionally broad, as you've just said?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, any statistics made on the basis of census data are simply not -- are complete. It is not that we have a large margin of error in this case, statistics compiled on the basis of the voters' register have very narrow confidence intervals meaning that uncertainty related to any statistics compiled based on the voters is extremely low. That is the effect of the very, very large size of this source. This is just reliable statistics that are obtained.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Can you tell us now what were the key pieces of data you used from each of these sources when preparing the IDP's and refugees report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: When preparing the statistics on displacement of the population, as I said individual data was used, basic items essential for this analysis included ethnicity and the place of residence or registration to vote in the case of the voters' register. But so that would be the ethnicity and place of residence or registration to vote. But in addition to this, these two sources in order to make the analysis had to be linked with each other, that is, records from the census and the voters' registers had to be matched and for this names of individuals listed in the census and in the voters' register were used. So that would be the next portion of information that was essential for this study. In addition to this, the individual identification number available in the population census and in the voter's register, the so-called JMBG was used in the matching procedure as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: You've just started --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, could I ask you one additional question. All the answers you've given, it is true that I find them all in the first part of your report "objective and scope," that's mainly what Mr. Farr is asking you about, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is all described in the report, partly in the objective and scope and largely in the annexes, methodological annexes and source-related annexes of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There we find the detail, but the level of questions put by Mr. Farr to you, let's say, 95 per cent answered in the objective and scope.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr, we've read that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, you just started describing the linking process that you used, and as Judge Orie has indicated, it's described in detail in your report. Can you tell us why you decided to use this method of linking records between your two large sources?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The method has its rationale in the idea of tracing individuals who lived in Bosnia at the outbreak of the conflict, that would be the individuals reported in the population census. Throughout I did a whole conflict period, war period, and until the post-conflict situation. So the linking process is just nothing else but tracing, looking to -- for what happened to the same individuals over time and in this particular case the place of residence, the changes in the place of residence were the central question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And how long did this process of matching records between the census and the voter register take?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: It was a very long process that started in 1998 and the project was finished in terms of matching and compiling basic statistics in mid-2003, so it took at least five years to complete these matching activities. Because of the size of the sources and because of the complexity of the practicalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And I think you just indicated that the place of residence was one of the key pieces of data that you compared between 1991 and 1997/1998; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Now in your report you deal with two kinds of numbers of internally displaced persons and refugees. Minimum numbers and estimated complete numbers. My question is: Do the matched records correspond to the minimum numbers or to estimated complete numbers?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The matched records correspond to the minimum numbers. The minimum numbers could be documented if required by lists of name of displaced persons, including their personal details before and after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Turning now to the estimated complete numbers, can you briefly describe how these numbers were obtained?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The estimated numbers -- the idea of the estimated numbers, first of all is related to the fact that the minimum numbers, as the name suggests, are very minimum, that means they are incomplete and shouldn't be seen as ultimate numbers of the displaced population. So in order to compensate for this deficiency of the minimum numbers, we estimated the more complete numbers for which we used some sampling statistics obtained based on the voters' register which were applied to the pre-war census population. It was a basic simple statistical procedure that should be seen as extrapolation of sample statistics over the entire pre-war population.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I'd like to turn now to the results of the IDP's and refugees report. But before that I wanted to ask you a few questions about the way in which you analysed the territory of the Stanisic-Simatovic area. The number of the results in the report are presented with respect to the portion of the territory that ended up in the RS versus the portion of the territory that ended up in the Federation. Can you briefly describe what portions of the five pre-war municipalities in the Stanisic-Simatovic area eventually became part of the RS and which eventually became part of the Federation?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. As a matter of fact, the municipalities covered by the indictment include just five pre-war municipalities. When I say pre-war implies that there is a post-war division of municipalities as well, and this post-war division we call post-Dayton division so the number of municipalities, the administrative division of the country into the municipalities obviously changed pre- and post-war periods. So the five municipalities, Bijeljina, Bosanski Samac, Zvornik, Doboj and Sanski Most, these five municipalities were correspond to 11 post-Dayton municipalities. What happened in the post-war division of municipalities, several municipalities were split into RS part and federal part. This happened to four out of the five municipalities included in this indictment. Bijeljina actually is the only one that has not been split; all other municipalities were split and Doboj was split into even four areas. So the RS municipalities relate to these parts of the pre-war municipalities that became part of Republika Srpska and the federal part is the one that belonged to the Federation. I think it is convenient to perhaps take a look at this stage at the population in the RS part and the federal part as reported in the population census, so the RS part was approximately 240.000 individuals and the federal part is about 80.000 individuals. So it is that the population in the RS part of the municipalities was much larger. These are the census data that are included in the report as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you, we'll now turn to the results of your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And Your Honours, I would direct your attention to the demonstrative exhibit of the excerpted results of the IDP's and refugees report that was handed out before court. That's document 65 ter 5862, and I'd ask that we can have that on e-court as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, I just have two introductory questions regarding this demonstrative exhibit and the other we'll be using today for the victims' report. First, is it correct that all the results in these demonstrative exhibits come from your reports themselves in the places indicated in the end notes to the demonstrative exhibits?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: It is also correct that the particular results presented in these demonstrative exhibits were selected by a process of consultation between you and members of the trial team?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: So looking at the demonstrative exhibit, let's start with table 1 of the summary of the IDP's and refugees report which divides the results according to the RS part and the FBiH part of the Stanisic and Simatovic area. The first row of the table is entitled, "Minimum numbers of IDP's and refugees." Can you briefly tell us what these numbers are?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The first row as you said contains the minimum numbers. These are the numbers of displaced population, internally displaced and externally displaced; internally meaning within Bosnia-Herzegovina and externally, outside Bosnia-Herzegovina. These numbers are the minimum numbers, that is, they come from the matching procedure and can be documented with personal and residence and ethnic details of every case included in these numbers. So the numbers are, first of all, given here only for the individuals that were born before 1980. This was a necessary restriction that had to be applied to both voters' registration and population census in order to make the statistics comparable over time. So it is the first remark. We have here two panels in this table. The first panel relates to displaced population from the RS part of the Stanisic-Simatovic area, and the second panel relates to the federal part of the Stanisic-Simatovic area. The Stanisic-Simatovic area are just five municipalities, pre-war municipalities, or alternatively as they were transformed into the 11 post-Dayton municipalities. So for the RS part the number mentioned in the table in the first row is approximately 56.000 individuals, exactly 55.837, 55.837. So that is the overall number of displaced population who used to live at the outbreak of the conflict in the RS parts of the Stanisic-Simatovic area. That is the first number. And further there is the ethnic breakdown of this number, so there is, for instance, 44.798 Muslim displaced persons, internally displaced and refugees, and 2.560 ethnic Serbs who became displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Tabeau. Moving to the next row, the second row is entitled, "Per Cent of IDP's and refugees within ethnic groups." Can you tell us conceptually what this number represents?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: This is a statistic obtained from the voters' records. For instance, 96 per cent that is given for the Muslim displaced persons means that 96 per cent of the population identified as of 1997/8, 96 per cent of this Muslim population became internally or externally displaced as of 1997/8.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Can I just ask a follow-up on that. I think I'm -- well, just tell me if this is correct, is it correct that for every 100 Muslims from the RS part of the Stanisic-Simatovic area for whom you were able to match records, 96 would have left their 1991 municipality of residence by 1997/1998?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, that's the interpretation. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And similarly for every 100 Serbs from the Federation part of the Stanisic Simatovic area for whom you were able to match records, 99.6 would have left their 1991 municipality of residence by 1997/1998?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Are these the numbers that are represented graphically by figure 2 at the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Is there anything in your data or other information that you are aware of that allows you to conclude whether these two significant population movements, that is, one of Muslims and one of Serbs, occurred at the same time or at different times?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Probably these movements were occurring more or less in the same time. I believe these were most likely parallel processes. I would think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: The next row is titled, "More complete number of IDP's and refugees." Earlier you described numbers that you developed using statistical estimation methods. Are those these numbers?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The more complete number is the estimated number and this, I said it is obtained by extrapolation, the sample proportion of displaced persons over the entire 1991 population.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And I think you, in addition to your estimated complete numbers, you also show a 95 per cent confidence interval for those numbers. I think you said earlier that a confidence interval is somehow related to the degree of certainty related to an estimation, but can you just tell us what these confidence intervals that you have for this estimate mean?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Confidence intervals indeed express the uncertainty related or associated with the point estimate. Point estimate is just one single number in this case of displaced persons, but of course it is just a point estimate and we are not 100 per cent sure that that is the number. So using certain statistical techniques, we can make confidence intervals which are telling us what would happen if many samples would be taken from a certain population and each time statistics, the same statistics would be calculated based on a different sample. So this confidence interval, for instance, for Muslims, it is 76.372 lower end, and upper end 76.708, this is an interval which with a high confidence, in this case 95 per cent confidence, comprises, contains the unknown number of displaced person, displaced Muslims in this case. It is a very narrow confidence interval which is related to the large size of the sample that would be the voters' register, and this kind of narrow confidence interval suggests that our point estimate is very precise, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that it would theoretically be possible to prepare a list of the individuals included in the minimum number by name and place of residence in the two relevant years. Now, correct me if I'm wrong, but my understanding that it would not be possible to do that with your estimated complete numbers; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, partly correct, partly not, because the more complete number as a matter of fact should be seen as containing the minimum number plus the correction, say, or additional component that can be obtained using statistical techniques. So for the minimum number, yes, but not for the additional part on the top of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: All right. Can we now move to the top of the next page and take a look at table 4. This also divides the results between the RS and the Federation. And I'll ask you some more detailed questions in a minute, can you just tell us briefly in general terms what table 4 sets out?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Table 4 summarises the ethnic composition in the RS and federal part of the Stanisic-Simatovic area. Ethnic composition on one hand is represented for 1991 and on the other hand it is the ethnic composition as of 1997. The ethnic composition is expressed first of all by absolute numbers and in addition to these in terms of percentage. It's important to note that the absolute numbers for 1991 are complete, but for 1997, it's again a sample. Large sample, but a sample. So the 1997 absolute numbers are not the size of the 1997 actual size of the 1997 population. Percentages however can be compared in these two years, so the second panel of this table, of table 4 for 1991 and 1997 can be directly compared and assessed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And that's the panel that is titled "Per cent"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And just to use an example to make this more concrete, is the correct way to read this table that the Muslim population in the RS part of the Stanisic-Simatovic area fell from 33.1 percentage points to 1.6 percentage points of the total population between 1991 and 1997 and that this represents a decrease of 95.3 per cent?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And at the same time the Serb population increased from just over half to just over 90 per cent of the population of the RS portion of the area?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That is an increase by 76.4 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Is it these changes in ethnic composition in percentage terms that are represented by figure 12 at the bottom of this page?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, I'd now like to ask you a few questions about a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Could we please have 65 ter number 564 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: This document has the heading of the Banja Luka Centre for State Security Department of the Republika Srpska MUP. It's dated February 1995, and it is titled, "Overview of data on the number and ethnic structure of population according to municipalities in the area of the Bahn Luke RDB centre for 1991 and 1995." This document was seised by the Prosecution on 27 February 1998, from the Security Services Centre in Banja Luka. Dr. Tabeau, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And you do have a copy of it in front of you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Can you briefly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it on our screen already?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In order to follow the evidence, it's good for us to have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently there's something wrong with the system. Nevertheless, Mr. Farr, if you would look at the screen as well, so you would know whether the Judges have access to the material you are asking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I can proceed to something else and come back to this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, we'll now turn to your victims report. I would first note that there are two main parts to this report, the first part is the body and the first three annexes which deal with all of the war-related victims from the Stanisic-Simatovic area. The second part is annex 4 which deals specifically with the victims whose murder are charged in this case. We'll deal with these two parts in that order, and again, we'll deal with sources, methodology, and findings. Starting with the main body of the report, pages 4 to 6 list the sources you use to compile the victims report. Can you briefly explain not what the sources are, because that's what is in the report already, but what qualities or characteristics of these sources led to you select them?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I think it's important to note that finding appropriate sources, reliable sources that would report on war victims is a very hard thing to do. So in the times of conflict, the expectation that sources are easily available, complete, and reliable and without any deficiencies is simply wrong. So the sources that we use -- the sources that we use are nevertheless the best we could identify and collect and should be seen as largely complete and reliable. We made a lot of efforts to acquire sources on both civilian and military victims of war. For instance, when it comes to the military victims, we have complete lists of fallen soldiers and other personnel associated with the ministries of defence in Bosnia and Herzegovina. When it comes to the -- should I continue? Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm still listening but at the same time I'm looking there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. So when it comes to sources related to civilians, we used two large databases that were compiled by the statistical authorities of Federation and Republika Srpska in Bosnia-Herzegovina in which they computerised at our request all death notifications from the time of the war. There were two groups of deaths in these sources. On one hand we had natural deaths that were excluded from this report and any other report related to victims of war. But the other part of information was explicitly reporting on victims of war. These lists, RS and FBiH lists, the so-called Dem 2 [phoen] databases on war-time mortality were importantly prepared by the professional statisticians with appropriate training and experience in providing these kind of information and secondly, these records are documented by, for instance, death certificates or other documents, for instance, court declarations of certain individuals to be dead. We also worked with lists of missing persons, which is an important source on victims of war. As long as there is no body of the deceased -- of a deceased this person cannot be included in the records of official death notifications, so including missing persons records is an important thing to do in this kind of project. We also worked with exhumation records, that would be the records of identification of victims whose bodies were found in the mass graves in Bosnia and Herzegovina. So the sources that we used, I most certainly believe were the best available for this kind of work and these are not just sources, these are appropriate sources that report on victims of war. They are reliable, large, however, I cannot say they are complete. They are incomplete, and of course, they are deficient as well in several ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: At page 3 of the victims' report you indicate that mortality sources were required to contain information on the date, place and cause of death or disappearance. Why did you require sources to contain this kind of information in order to be used?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, generally we require any source to be the individual-level source, that means information must be available on persons. That means, basically, these are long lists of victims, dead or missing persons or exhumed or identified persons, and for in order to be able to process this information and to cross-reference sources and eliminate duplication, we first of all need to have personal details, like names, date of birth, place of birth, et cetera, and in order to study the details of their death or disappearance, we need to have information about date, place, cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And why is cause of death, in particular, important?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, cause of death is important because we are speaking of victims of war, that is, the causes of death are, of course, violent in this case, and cause of death is important not to mix natural death with violent war-related deaths.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Is it correct that you looked only at violent war-related deaths?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I said, the subject of our study were the violent war-related deaths.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I would now like to turn to your methodology. In section 3 of the victims' report you mention the 2010 integrated database and you describe how it was constructed using your 12 sources. You also mention two additional sources, one of which is the 1991 population census and the second of which are the 1997/1998 and 2000 voter registers. Starting with the 1991 population census, can you tell us how that was used and what it was used for in the creation of the 2010 integrated database?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Perhaps I will come to this, but it's important to say what the integrated mortality database is. This is a database that covers all war-related deaths that we were able to identify in the course of time in our sources, in the demographic unit. This database was put together very recently, so its final version was available, became available, in, I believe, January this year. So it summarises the results of our work with sources reporting on war victims, the work experience which is, as I think, about ten years long as of now. This database covers the entire war in Bosnia and Herzegovina and entire territory of the country. So this database was a match of 12 large sources on victims of war and, of course, eliminating the duplications, overlap of sources, cleaning the data, repairing gaps if possible, et cetera, et cetera. That is the crucial part of the core of our work, but in order to make sure that all these victims were indeed living in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the outbreak of the conflict, the census population of 1991 is used. We cross-reference the victims with the census population in order to validate the personal details of the victims, and possibly to expand the record of information on every person by including census information in the records on deaths or disappearance. So the role of census and validation and improving information about the war victims. On the other hand, there is the other group of sources. This would be the sources reporting on the surviving population, that would be the voters' registers of 1997, 1998, 2000. We also have the register, official register of internally displaced persons and refugees of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina; it's another source of surviving population. So what we do is, as well, cross-referencing the lists of victims of war with the records of surviving population. This is done in order to eliminate false positives that would be the persons reported dead or missing who at the same time are obvious survivors. So that is the methodology that we used for this project and for several other projects. Importantly, of course, not all the records were used from the integrated database which is a large database. It's altogether about 90.000 records of war victims from Bosnia. We extracted the relevant records from this database using the criterion of area and time, as exactly defined in this indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: At pages 8 to 9 of the victims report, you indicate that information on ethnicity was not universally available from mortality sources, but that information on ethnicity could be obtained from the 1991 census for those records that were matched with the census. Just to be clear, did you take any information on ethnicity from the mortality sources or did you always take it from the 1991 census?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: We always take it from the population census and one is that it is not -- ethnicity is not universally reported but more importantly we realise that ethnicity is, as a matter of fact, self-perception that may change over time, depending on the circumstances one lives in. So in order to eliminate any bias related to changing perceptions of ethnicity, we also always ethnicity obtained on the basis of links with the population census. So it's ethnicity as reported in the 1991 census, not biased by any changes of -- in later reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: The victims' report also contains information regarding the military or civilian status of the victims, and you explain in the report the way that you assigned military status to certain victims. You also indicated at page 9 of the victims' report that this designation does not correspond necessarily to combatants, why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The approach we have been applying for many years now is that any victim included in the military lists -- we have three military lists, the lists of ABiH soldiers, VRS soldiers, ABH soldiers, that are the three factions involved, military factions involved in the conflict. So we have these lists, altogether, I believe 54.000 records. These lists were made for the purpose of postmortem benefits to the families of the persons included, so whoever is confirmed, whoever of our victims is confirmed in these lists, we assign this person the status "military." But it has nothing to do with the circumstances -- or it has something to do but not -- there is no one-to-one correspondence between the circumstances of death and the fact of being reported a military in the sense of our definition. What I'm trying to say being a military doesn't mean that a person died in combat circumstances. It just means that the person was associated in some way with the army or the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure exactly what time we started, I don't know if this is an appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We usually have a break after 75 minutes, but I'm more concerned about the way your last question -- first of all, we know that Ms. Tabeau worked on the job for five years. I don't know what the relevance would have been if she worked on it for three years or seven years, mainly looking at the quality of her work and that's, so therefore that's a totally superfluous question. Apart from that, the military status whether or not in combat or whatever, I find that on page 9, military status is clearly explained. One line: "Among the soldiers a number of them died in combat but we have good reasons to believe that many died in non-combat situation. They were executed and their bodies exhumed from the mass graves." That's exactly what we spent two or three minutes on which you read in half a line and so clearly explains by the expert that I really wonder why we have not adopted as many other Chambers that if there is clear evidence on paper we should not spend too much time in first, seek the witness to be cross-examined. Mr. Farr, you've got ten more minutes until the break, do you think that with this in the back of your mind that you conclude the examination-in-chief of Ms. Tabeau? And perhaps look at your questions, see to what extent it's just repetition of what we tried hard to read because until now 40 per cent of your questions are really just what is clearly explained and the remaining 60 per cent you may have some doubt as whether we understood these statistics and what it all meant, there's a fair chance that we did, but I can imagine that you did not want to take any risk in that respect. Mr. Farr, you've ten more minutes, see how far you can come in those ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, I'd now like to turn to the results of your victims report.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I draw your attention to the document entitled, "Main findings of the victims report" that was handed out before court and I would note for the record that this document has been uploaded as 65 ter 5863.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, at the top of this demonstrative exhibit we see the minimum number and estimated overall number that come from your victims' report. Can I just ask you, is it correct that for this minimum number it would theoretically be possible to prepare a list naming each of those victims as it is for the minimum number in the IDP's and refugees report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it is practically possible, not only theoretically. It's practically possible, we do have the lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Tabeau. Moving to the estimated overall --

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And Your Honour, I'll be guided by the Chamber whether any clarification is required with respect to the way in which the estimated overall number was calculated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Seems to be clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, turning to table 3B at the bottom of the page, please tell me if I'm interpreting this correctly. In the middle section where it says, "percentages by ethnicity," and looking at the column that says "civilians" is the correct way to read this table that of the minimum number of 3.092 civilians, 73 per cent were Muslim, 19.2 per cent were Serb, 3.7 per cent were Croats and 3.4 per cent were others?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And is it also correct that within the minimum number of 5.359 Muslim victims, for example, 42.5 per cent were civilians and 57.5 per cent had military status?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: You've described the way in which the undercount was calculated in your report. Can you please just tell us what the undercount indicates, if anything, about the reliability of the minimum number?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The minimum number is the list of victims that we can document using the information from our sources, but there is a number of exclusions from -- that could not be extracted as relevant to the Stanisic-Simatovic indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, I apologise for interrupting you. I believe that that's explained in your report. Could you just tell us, what, if anything, the estimated undercount tells us about the reliability of the minimum number?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, the -- we tried to by presenting in quantitative terms the undercount of our minimum number, we expressed, we made an attempt to express what part is missing in this number. So that it is the minimum number is incomplete is obvious because we have been applying very conservative approach, excluding deficient records, rejecting sources that are not reliable enough, that we believe are biased, et cetera, et cetera. So but it is not only that we have done all these exclusions but we also know that sources are incomplete. So the undercount estimate actually is a quantitative expression of the missing part in the minimum number.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Could I summarise that or could I conclude that the existence of this estimated undercount in some way illustrates that the minimum number is a conservative number?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, that is the confirmation of it as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, I'd now like to turn to annex 4 of the victims' report. This is the portion that deals specifically with the victims whose murder is charged in the indictment in this case. And I'll first just ask you background, a few background questions regarding the kinds of documents that you reviewed in the course of preparing the charts that form part of annex 4. You list these documents at pages 3 and 4, these kinds of documents at pages 3 and 4 of annex 4 and I'll just ask you very briefly, can you estimate how many documents of these kinds you've looked at during your work with the OTP?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I think the number of documents that were reviewed in our project, proof of that project was 250 plus-minus a few, but 250 documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Is that with respect to the victims in this case?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: This is the documents that were -- that are covering, that covered the victims of listed in the schedules to the indictment. Only this group of victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: My question was more general, during the course of your ten years of work in the Office of the Prosecutor, how many documents of these types have you had the opportunity to look at?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I've been working with these kinds of documents systematically as my unit is the one that is responsible for the OTP exhumations project so we've been in touch, and I personally have been in touch with organisations issuing these kind of reports, like the state commission for tracing missing persons, in fact that the International Commission for Missing Persons in Sarajevo, and also for other cases of this be Tribunal, Srebrenica cases for instance, Krajina cases, these type of documents have been used systematically.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Could we say that you've reviewed thousands of documents of this type during your work at the OTP?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that would be probably the case. I wouldn't be able to say how many thousand but many, many documents of this kind have gone through my hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And during the course of reviewing these documents, have you become familiar with their usual form, the functional position that would usually be held by a person who would sign or prepare them, the specific organisations that and the specific organisations that created them in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course, I as well personally visited several organisations involved in the exhumation and identification processes in Bosnia and Herzegovina, so it is not only that I had opportunity to studies the actual documents, I also had the opportunity to speak to persons who participated in exhumations and issued the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I'd now like to move to the charts appearing in annex 4 to the victims' report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one question perhaps. You said you reviewed some 250 documents here. I'm looking at page 3 of annex 4, "Overview of exhumation and identification documents used as proof of death," you come to 430. Is it -- that's not the same as 250 or that's just a rough guess or... What explains the difference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, on this table as a matter of fact the 430 are links to documents, so there were a number of bigger documents that contained lists of victims. So this increases the number of actual documents when we speak of document links to victims to 430. So there were actually 250 documents but because some of them were associated with more than one victim, then if we rearrange the documents, associated document with every victim then this increases the number of the actual documents to the document links, that is 430. That means --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, total documents is the total number of links with documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, to every single victim from the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where it may be in one document you find ten links where it's still only one document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So where you say that for one victim you sometimes have more documents, what you could have added is that sometimes one document you have more victims.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, I'd now like to move to the charts appearing in annex 4 to the victims report.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And obviously that's all been passed out to the parties and the Chamber before court but could we please have page 7 of the second document linked to 65 ter 5748 on the screen for the benefit of the public?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, can you tell us what each row of this chart represents?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: This is one row in this table relates as a matter to fact to one victim, and for this particular victim it relates to a given, to a particular document in which details of the death or disappearance of this person are described. So for victim number 1, this is Ivan Agatic, Agatic Ivan, father's name Ante, there are two documents that were associated with this particular victim and are presented in this chart as two proof of death documents for this person. So the document order, the item called "Document order" for Agatic, there is document order 1 and document order 2. This item indicates how many documents were associated with every victim. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you. So essentially one row is one document and when there are multiple rows for one victim then that means there are multiple documents for that victim; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: This may be self-evident but can you tell us what it means when the word "yes" appears in the authenticity column with respect to a document?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: This comment means that this was a standard document that I was familiar with and I did recognise as a -- yeah, as systematically presented by authorities at various occasions and, the yes is just my yes to the authenticity, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I'd now like to go through the notations --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, we don't object to Mr. Farr continuing later, but we would ask if we could have a break, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Farr, could you tell us how much time you would still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Less than 20 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: After the break you have 15 minutes, Mr. Farr. We take a break and we'll resume at five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber apologises for the late start. Mr. Farr, the 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, I'd now like to go through the notations that we find in the column entitled, "Comment of Dr. Ewa Tabeau in the proof of death chart." And again being mindful of the time, I would ask you to give the shortest possible answer that is complete and accurate. Starting with the "associated POD" notation, what does that comment mean?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: "Associated POD" means, in full, associated proof of death document, and associated is related to a group of documents, exactly 38, which had the name of victims handwritten on the front page. Other than that, the name of the victim was not included in the text, body text, of the document. "Associated" means simply that it is just one of the documents related to a given victim, and the link between this document and other documents was established based on, exactly speaking, body label attached to the body of this victim and mentioned in the associated POD, as well as other documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you, what about the notation "reliable POD"?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: "Reliable POD" means that this was a regular proof of death document and victims' details were included in the body text in the standard form could be clearly seen from the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: What about "confirmed war victim," what does that notation mean?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: This means that the record of the same victim was found in the integrated mortality database and in brackets the numbers are related with subsequent sources in which this record was confirmed. For instance, in the third row, for the victim Antunovic, Jozo, document number 2, there is - and 1 as well - there is in the brackets the number 2, 3 which mean that is the same victim was reported in the integrated database in the underlying source number 2 and underlying source number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And that was list of sources is found on page 5 of annex 4; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Moving on to the next notation, what does "confirmed personal details" mean?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: This means that the record of this individual was found in the the population census 1991, so a match could be established between victim record and the census.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Now, moving to the column entitled "final conclusion." Under what circumstances did you put the entry "very satisfactory" in that column?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: These were cases for which I could conclude that it was a reliable proof of death document, that the victim record was confirmed in the integrated mortality database, and finally that this person's record was found in the population census.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Does your conclusion "very satisfactory" relate only to the fact of the person's death or does it also relate to other matters?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: There were two victims for whom only a missing person report was available and no other documents, and for these two persons, "very satisfactory" simply relates to the fact that there is a satisfactory record of missing for this person, not of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And with respect to the other individuals for whom you've said very satisfactory, does that relate only to the fact of the death or does it also relate to other matters, and if so which other matters?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, very satisfactory relates to the documents themselves, type and number of them, and the fact that the same victim could be confirmed in other sources of information, population census is important and the integrated mortality database.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And under what circumstances did you use the entry "satisfactory"?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: So these were cases for which the information was limited, for instance, there was no link established with the population census or integrated mortality database, and for associated POD documents, the 38 I mentioned with 100 names on the front page.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I'd now like to ask you about the 14 additional victims that you identified while reviewing the proof of death documentation. How did you identify those additional victims and why did you associate them with the other named victims?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jordash, before we entered court I said to my colleagues, we have not given Mr. Jordash his five minutes. I had on my mind to do it at the end of the examination-in-chief, but this might be a good moment as well. Ms. Tabeau, there was a procedural issue which does not directly affect you but I do not think there was any problem if Ms. Tabeau would listen to you, would it, if you make a submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, I think that must be right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then perhaps we since we are now moving to the 14 additional victims, that we give an opportunity to Mr. Jordash to raise the matter he wants to raise. And you've still got ten minutes left, Mr. Farr. Mr. Jordash, I had five minutes in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'll do my best. The application is to -- for Your Honours to order the Prosecution that if they wish to add 14 victims to the indictment against the accused they do so by applying to amend the indictment, rather than the intended process, which is to, as they've done, to apply to add the victims to the Rule 65 ter exhibit list in the filing of the 1st of October, 2010 and then seek to adduce the evidence through Ms. Tabeau, and thereby create an additional liability for the accused. And it is an additional liability for the accused in so far as what the Prosecution seek to do is increase the number of unlawful killings by 10 per cent. And in our submission, that must be done in a way which allows the parties to make submissions to Your Honours as to the prejudice which arises by that intention and application, and that must be done, in our submission, through an application to amend the indictment. The Prosecution's position is, as far as I understand it, that they may do it, they may add these victims firstly in the way that I've just outlined, and secondly, because the indictment annex E part 2 has a permitting phrase, as they would see it, where, for example, the victim list for Bosanski Samac names 16 victims and then has at the bottom with asterisks at the side of it "plus additional victims." And the same goes for Doboj and Sanski Most and Zvornik. In our submission, there's clear authority, and Your Honours, I rely upon Kupreskic appeal judgement, but I also rely upon the series of cases which followed Kupreskic in which -- has Your Honours received a copy of the -- I think your learned Registrar has the copies to be given to Your Honours, it's Kupreskic appeal judgement, paragraphs 88 to 90. And stated in straightforward terms, the Prosecution must state the victims on an indictment. There is an exception, a very narrow exception which arises in cases of mass-scale crimes, and in those instances the jurisprudence doesn't require each victim to be named. And if Your Honours look at paragraph 88, that sheer scale exception is referred to: "Obviously there may be instances where the sheer scale of the alleged crimes makes it impracticable to require a high degree of specificity in such matters as identity of the victims and the date for the commission of the crimes." And then as an illustration of what a sheer scale or what a -- the type of scale that the jurisprudence has in mind, Your Honours can see at paragraph 80 an example there of where an accused is alleged to participate as a member of an execution squad in the killings -- in the killing of hundreds of men. And if one then looks at our indictment, we fall, in our submission, well outside of that exception. Bosanski Samac, the Prosecution have named 16 victims, Doboj 20, Sanski Most 11 -- I beg your pardon, Sanski Most 36, and so on. In our submission, it is -- it was well within the possibility that the Prosecution could specify these victims and name them prior to the case commencing at the time the indictment was drafted. And to do so now or to attempt to do so now, one, without applying to amend the indictment is in principle wrong, and, two, if that application was to be made, in our submission it ought to fail on the basis that the sheer scale exception cannot be said to apply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr, Mr. Groome, whom should I attend at this moment? Please, Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I'll just respond on a couple of points. First of all, with respect to the applicability of Kupreskic, I'm speaking off the top of my head to some extent, but I believe that that related to more or less to the events of a single day in Ahmici. It was a geographically and temporally limited incident and the accused were direct perpetrators or very nearly direct perpetrators. We would submit that this is a much different case, this a much larger case and it's a case in which the that's more like the exception that Mr. Jordash was referring to than it is like Kupreskic. Just specifically with respect to the incidents with respect to which new victims have been identified, in the indictment schedule for Doboj we say, "plus additional victims," and only one additional victim has been identified. With respect to Zvornik, we say, "plus additional victims," and there it's a different situation, eight new victims have been identified. However page 62 of the indictment does charge the killing of approximately 20 non-Serb civilians, and I believe that these additional victims bring the number up to 26, if I'm not mistaken. The final example is the example of Sasina and Sanski Most. In that situation we, in fact, plead only plus one additional victim and Dr. Tabeau has identified five new victims. So that's a situation which I think we would concede that we might be required to amend the indictment. Or be guided by the Chamber as to how else we might proceed by filing new victims list or whatever is appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Briefly in our submission, Mr. Farr doesn't address the nub of the issue. One has to break down the crime bases. Was it impracticable for the Prosecution when naming 16 victims relating to the Bosanski Samac crime base to name a handful more and give the Defence an ample opportunity to deal with those alleged killings throughout the whole of the Prosecution case rather than at the end of it. And secondly, it isn't an issue in our submission with concerning how large the additional victim list. It's an issue of an addition. The Prosecution may say, well, we are only adding one unlawful killing. Well, that's one unlawful killing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You started talking about percentages, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Only to show the gravity of the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, so apparently there the quantity, not to say exclusively, has some importance to you as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It has some importance for those who are prejudiced by it. It doesn't have importance for those who are benefitting from it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Benefitting is perhaps not ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Perhaps that's not the right word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand what you mean, in whose favour it would be. So the issue, if I could summarise it briefly, is the following: We are talking about the relevance of this evidence because it's the position of Mr. Jordash that in order to name victims which were not named at any earlier stage, that this would require an amendment of the indictment for which the Chamber should give its approval, whereas, Mr. Farr, you take the position that it's just filling in names for until now unidentified persons. I don't know whether I've missed it, the 14 additional victims, the identity is here of course established, it's part of the list now, when did the Office of the Prosecution identify who they were?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau identified the additional victims as she was preparing annex 4 to the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then perhaps the question to you, annex 4 exactly was prepared when? It may be that I said I read everything, but I might miss some details.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The date is 23rd of September, 2010. That is the date of the report and this is when the work was finished and it became obvious that these are new entries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You linked them to the incidents by name, so that was -- without this knowledge, the Prosecution could not have named them at any earlier stage. I think we have to further look at the case law. It is my recollection that in the Gotovina case a similar matter played a role, although the scale was perhaps not exactly the same. Kupreskic, the scale is also not the same but perhaps at the other end of the scale. I suggest that the Chamber will consider the objection and, Mr. Jordash, it finally comes down to the relevance of the evidence on the 14, isn't it, because if they are not included in the indictment, it is at least to prove killed victims in the indictment, it would be irrelevant because they would not be covered by it. You say you first should name them, ask for an amendment of the indictment and then we'll oppose and then therefore whether it's -- this is relevant evidence or not depends on how we should look at the indictment and there the parties are 180 per cent opposed. You say it's not part of the indictment if the indictment is not amended. Mr. Farr says these are the unnamed but meanwhile known victims we refer to already in the indictment and therefore covered by the indictment. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think that is the position, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If that is the case, then I suggest that we would continue, that the Chamber considers whether Mr. Jordash is right or Mr. Farr is right on whether, in order to make these 14 victims in the indictment, whether the indictment should be amended or not, and then of course, we'll draw consequences as far as the evidence is concerned how relevant and how probative it is for what has to be proven.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, I agree with what Your Honour has just said, but may I just add this, that I think the situation is more complicated though than the indication just given by Ms. Tabeau. For example in relation to when the victims names were discovered or discoverable, and I say that because I'm in possession of 65 ter 4871 and there is the name of one victim there, I don't think there's a problem saying his name in open court, Omar Delic, who was named in a document to Mr. Brammertz, the chief Prosecutor on the 5th of June, 2008, and he is one of the 14. So in our submission, the Prosecution ought to at least set out with some specificity when it is they came into possession of each name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which raises another matter, that I don't know what document you are referring to, but if one sends a letter and says A, B, or C was killed at that same moment, if you have no other evidence whether you should immediately amend the indictment or not or whether... Again, I do not know what the document exactly is about, but not the mere fact that a name is mentioned in a document would justify to seek an amendment of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I completely agree. I'm just submitting that the situation is more complex than that indicated by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's any way for the parties to agree on these kind of factual matters which are underlying the more principled arguments so that we don't have to -- of course, if you disagree on those matters, whether you could or could not have earlier identified those persons, then of course we'd have to take that into consideration as well when deciding upon your application, if that is a relevant answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We would still, of course, say, even if they couldn't, there ought to be a proper opportunity for the Defence to lay out any prejudice which arises from the late discovery of victims names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would prefer to receive brief written submissions on the matter. We are talking about the scope of the indictment, what is covered by the indictment, what is not covered by the indictment, which is of course always a fundamental issue in a case and therefore the parties are invited to make brief submissions. How much time would you need for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, if the Prosecution as the moving party were to file their submissions, we could respond within a very short time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You are the moving party here, isn't it, Mr. Farr? You want to add this information to the 65 ter list, suddenly the 14 pop up and --

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I believe there's a motion pending already to add the documents to the 65 ter list but we are happy to file submissions first, that's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course what we could do is first ask Mr. Jordash to respond to that and give you an opportunity to reply. If you already would make an additional filing in which you explain your point of view as you just did on under what circumstances the exception applies and then Mr. Jordash will have an opportunity to respond to the motion in its entirety, whether there will be any need to have a second round, we'll see once we've read your submissions. Meanwhile, Mr. Jordash, I don't think it's prejudicial if we would continue at this moment hearing the evidence. I mean, either it's relevant or it's not relevant, and it's only 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. The Simatovic Defence shares the position of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. My learned friend Mr. Jordash spoke on behalf of our Defence team as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we'd like to receive your submissions by Friday close of business. That's the 10th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, can you please tell us as briefly as possible, how you identified these additional victims and how did you associate them with the victims already on the list for the given incidents?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The one victim from Doboj was included based on the letter mentioned already from the V8 [phoen] Prosecutor's Office to the Prosecutors of ICTY Serge Brammertz, and in addition to these there was an exhumation report in which several other victims were listed. This exhumation report relates to the Makljenovac sites. Other victims were already included in the indictment list except for this one so that is the reason that I decided to consider this person as a new victim. For Sasina, there are 5 reports and five new victims, all of them are declarations, court declarations of the lower court in Sanski Most declaring these individuals dead and death circumstances as related to the Sasina incident. There are witness statements summarised in these declarations which all confirm the relevance of the circumstances of death to the Sasina incident from the indictment. Finally in relation to Zvornik, the eight victims were included based on the identification reports for these victims. Each of these reports includes partly information from the families and as well DNA matching results confirming the identity of these victims. So there is a date of that report here and the place of death and they are all related to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you. One of the additional victims you identified is Munevera Resic. Since identifying her as an additional victim, have you changed your opinion with respect to her?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it at some point when cross-referencing documents related to this victim and another victim, well, at that time we thought another victim, it was Munevera Alagic, as far as I remember, yes, Alagic, from the document related to the Munevera Resic, obviously it was a court declaration with some witness statements, one of the persons giving the statement was her husband, Mr. Resic, it became obvious that the maiden name of the person was Alagic, so it was Resic that was the name the person acquired through the marriage.
