utterances.text: I would next tender the underlying documents listed on the proof of death chart for victims other than the additional victims. Unfortunately, I don't know exactly what the number of those documents is, I only have an overall number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you prepare the list, give it to Madam Registrar, Madam Registrar will provide numbers to it. But could I hear already whether there would be any objection against the underlying documents, if not, you are requested to proceed as I suggested, Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Finally, we would just ask for at the same time the remaining documents with respect to the additional victims to be MFI'd as well, pending resolution of the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you also make a list of those and that should undergo the same fate as -- that means those numbers are assigned for purposes at this moment for marking for identification. Anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Mr. Bakrac, is it you or is it Mr. Jordash who will go first?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, your guess was right. I'm going to go first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Bakrac is counsel for Mr. Simatovic. Please proceed, there seems to be an additional noise in my earphones. There was one moment when it disappeared, but I don't know what changed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's my microphone that's causing the noise. I'll try using the other one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But at this moment -- okay. Please proceed the best possible way using the best microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I don't know how much the microphone is going to help me but I'm going to do my best to continue in the best possible way, right. Good afternoon, Ms. Tabeau, I have a few questions for you in order to clarify certain matters, both for our Defence and for the Trial Chamber actually. I'm going to focus on the first part of your report now that speaks about ethnic composition and internally displaced persons and refugees from six municipalities, that's what it says here, but actually reference was made to five municipalities from 1991 until 1997 or 1998. Actually, my understanding was that these municipalities, these five municipalities after Dayton became a different number of municipalities, but is that what we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you are looking at the old version of the report. I actually have in the title five municipalities. This is one point. But indeed the five municipalities were split and resulting municipalities are post-Dayton municipalities and there were 11 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Very well. Ms. Tabeau, if I understand you correctly, this is a report that pertains to the entire period from 1991 up until 1997, or rather 1998; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Again if I've understood you correctly, Ms. Tabeau, the basis for your report, or rather, the two basic foundations of your report are the census of Bosnia-Herzegovina for 1991, and the voters' list compiled after the Dayton Accords in 1997 and 1998. On the basis of these two fundamental sources, you compiled your report; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: These were the major sources. There were additional as well, but these were the major, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: If I understood things correctly, this document from Banja Luka from 1995, I don't know whether it's the public security centre or the state security centre, I'm not sure now, but that is the additional document that you used; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, in addition to these basic sources and this additional one that our learned friend Mr. Farr showed us, could you tell us what else you know concerning demographic figures or documents or evidence that in a demographic sense reflects what happened in 1992, 1993, 1994, 1995, and 1996 in the territory of these five municipalities that were later split up on the basis of the Dayton Accords?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: We have another source that I also used as contextual in my report, this is the BH government registration of internally displaced persons and refugees in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and these persons registered in that source are all related to the events during the conflict 1992 to 1995. And I am aware of another document by the Ministry of the Interior, state security sector, related to 1993 which unfortunately I didn't use in this particular report but in which there is mention or there are reports about the population movements from the municipalities in the Banja Luka sector. I mean, population movements, mainly outflow of the population of ethnicities other than Serbs and inflow of population of Serb ethnicity. So there are some documents. I'm sure that many more documents could be identified. I am aware of a number of UNHCR documents, reports, monitoring reports, further monitoring reports of other international monitors that were reporting on the population movements during the conflict period. I didn't use them all in this particular report. Why? Because it is far more reliable to use primary sources like the census and the voters' register and compile statistics from individual data. This is something that one can have full control of, and moreover, every displaced person can be documented by information from these sources. So context is one thing, and there are quite a number of, a large number of sources that can be used to discuss the context in terms of aggregate statistics, but using primary sources, individual micro-level sources and making statistics based on these sources is a totally different thing. It is a far more reliable, more specific, well-defined approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, you explained to us why you hadn't used these other sources, why you ignored them. I would be interested in the following: While you compiled your report, did you have information to the effect that towards the end of 1991 for instance, from the area of Western Slavonia, about 40.000 refugees, Serbs, came to the area of Banja Luka? Did you include that in your report when you provided the final figure of 1997, 1998 about the census? Actually, the ballot and the persons who were eligible to vote?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, I did not have records of the refugees from Western Slavonia. I believe these records could have been obtained somehow. It was not my purpose to collect them. However, the, yeah, refugees from Western Slavonia wouldn't be citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina, right? So that is a totally different group of population, so the target population of my report was the population who resided in Bosnia in 1991 and demographic consequences of the conflict to this population.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But, Ms. Tabeau, let us take the assumption that out of these 40.000, say, 20.000 in the meantime received Bosnian documents, that is to say, documents of the Republika Srpska, and were therefore on the voters' register of 1997 and 1998. Would that not affect the ratio and the number that you presented to us in your report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: No, no, this is not as you are saying. In order to be registered as an eligible voter in 1997/1998 elections one had to be included in the population census in 1991. Unless one could demonstrate using IDs and other documents that this person even though not registered was the citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time. So as a matter of fact, it was a precondition, you know, to participate in the elections to be the citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1991 of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: As for your report, Ms. Tabeau, did you incorporate in it the 250.000 refugees from Croatia who came to the area of Banja Luka after Operation Flash and the same number came after Operation Storm? Did you look at that number of persons, Serbs who fled from the Krajina area? Did you take that into account when you worked on your statistical analysis?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I think it is wrong to say that the refugees in such large numbers, 250.000 Croatian Serbs came to Bosnia-Herzegovina. As far as I know, they did not come to Bosnia-Herzegovina in these large numbers. They did come to Serbia, and there are statistics reporting on these numbers. Statistics that show the country of origin of these refugees as well as the time of arrival in Serbia. So the largest numbers of Croatian Serbs ended in Serbia, not in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Well, again, this is the same issue. In order to participate in the elections of 1997/1998 one had to be listed on the population census of 1991. One had to be the citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina. My statistics are not flawed because of the alleged high numbers of refugees from Croatia that you are telling entered in Bosnia. I don't think so. First of all, there were not that many in Bosnia and Herzegovina as the many country of destination of the Croatian Serbs was Serbia, not Bosnia. There were some thousands and they are reported in the BH registration of IDP's and refugees, but it's not 250.000, it is 25.000 as of the year 2000, so it is a totally different number. But as I'm saying, it is the 1991 census population who must be taken into account when speaking of the election 1997/1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, very well, we are not going to debate the figures. You do allow for the possibility of some 25.000 Croatian Serbs remaining in the territory of these municipalities. My question is as follows: When you worked on your final figure of the number of Serbs in these municipalities in 1997 and 1998, did you find all of these persons on the list of persons in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1991? I mean the census, that's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, the matching rate for the voters with the population census is 80 per cent, so that means 80 per cent of records of the voters from the registered 1997/1998 were confirmed in the population census. It wasn't 100 per cent. There were 20 per cent that were not matched, basically because of deficiencies in the data. But I'm telling you once again, in principle the voters 1997/1998 had to be listed in the population census, moreover I can assure you that every registration office in Bosnia-Herzegovina during the elections had two copies of the population census, one was the hard copy, one was the electronic copy. And when people were coming to register to vote they had to prove they were on the census lists. So that is how it worked. It was the first serious democratic elections in 1997, after the 1996 election basically wasn't perfect as we know, right, and things were prepared in such a way that any fraud would be prevented and this is why the relationship between the census and the voters' list.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, but if I understood you correctly, you included in your figure these 20 per cent of the Serbs who were not on the census at all in 1991. The census of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that's what I'm talking about, or did you simply ignore that figure in your report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: My statistics are based on matched records, so only the 80 per cent matched are included in statistics. The 20 per cent unmatched are not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, do you remember, or can you tell us now, what was the number either in terms of numbers or in terms of percentage points in the census in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1991, how many Yugoslavs were there in terms of numbers or percentages?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I cannot say it from my head. I would have to check but it wasn't significant. The percentages of the two major groups, Bosniaks that would be the Muslims and the Serbs were considerable but not the percent of Yugoslavs. I don't recall the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, I would not agree with you. I think that Bosnia-Herzegovina was the republic that had the largest percentage of Yugoslavs in that period of time, however, the conclusion is that you cannot tell us now what the actual number was. Can you tell us how you treated such persons? Is it possible that some of these persons who were Yugoslavs in 1991, in the 1991 census, came to vote in 1997 and 1998 and was on the voters' register?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: As I mentioned earlier today, there were 98 categories, ethnic categories reported in the 1991 census. We regrouped the categories and created four major groups: Muslims, Serbs, Croats and others. Muslims, Serbs and Croats, three major groups, were taken as reported in the census without any modifications. The others is a large category that comprises among others the Yugoslavs, and many many other categories imported in the census. And one more remark I have that you said that Bosnia had relatively highest numbers of Yugoslavs, it might not mean that this number was very high. It is relatively high as compared to other republics, so it might be so but it doesn't mean that they were 40 per cent of Yugoslavs living in Bosnia and Herzegovina because they were not the major group in that republic, former republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Tabeau. If I understood you correctly, actually let me just try to confirm this, in your research, you established that there was more or less parallel population movement in that period. If we look at the percentage of Muslims or non-Serbs who left the area of Republika Srpska, if that is 96 per cent and if the number of Serbs who left the area of the Federation where the population is predominantly Muslim and Croat, the percentage is 99.6 per cent, did I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, I recall these two percentages and I agree it was a parallel movement. Serbs were moving out from the Federation and non-Serbs from the others' territory, this is the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Madam, Ms. Tabeau, in view of your rich experience as a scholar, can you tell us in situations or circumstances that prevailed then in the territory that was the focus of your study, was that customary in view of all the hotbeds of crisis that you analysed?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: If you could be more specific, what do you mean by circumstances that prevailed? So there was a conflict, a war going there in the territory of the country, certain areas were affected more than other areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That is what I'm saying. In these five municipalities during this period of time that we are discussing, there was a war going on among the ethnic groups there and that conflict practically engulfed all of Bosnia. In view of your experience, you said yourself that it seemed to you that this migration went along parallel lines, so in this situation of ethnic fighting, conflicts, is it logical that, say, Muslim inhabitants are going into areas where the population is predominantly Muslim and the other way around, that Serbs go to areas where the population is predominantly Serb when there is a war going on?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, I think what I meant when saying that there was war in these territories, most certainly there were combat activities, but most certainly there were incidences of mass violence and from the victim's report, it is clear that the Muslims were the major group who actually suffered in the war and mass violence incidents as well. Well, I am not, you know, I don't feel okay to say that it is normal that large groups of population moved this way or that way in war. I don't think these movements are voluntary because there must be some factors that force people out from their homes. Why? Because numbers of people who moved were so extremely high, so the situation must have been dramatic in order to push them out and leave their homes. And if there are killings and large numbers of killings, we are speaking of about 10.000 excess deaths related to war in these territories in the war period so that is not neglectible [sic], it is a high number of predominantly Muslim population who actually suffered in this war and mass violence incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, I do apologise, it's probably that I used a clumsy term when I said normal. I actually meant customary, usual. When you spoke about suffering now, actually, in order to leave your home, you assume that it has to do with forcible expulsions, when you are talking about Muslims, you are also referring to those Serbs who left the Federation, over 90 per cent of them; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: That is the number, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Tabeau, as you worked on your statistics, and we all know that sometime in November 1995 the Dayton Agreement was signed, peace was established on the the basis of the Dayton Agreement, right? And did the Dayton Agreement return the right to every refugee to go back to his or her place of residence, his or her home, are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it was part of the Dayton Agreement, the right to return home.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I think this is a very important question. When we are supposed to make such judgements about forcible expulsions, et cetera. Did you devote your report or part of your report to facts and figures pertaining to the number of Muslims who returned to their homes after the Dayton Agreement or how many Serbs or how many Croats returned to their homes after the Dayton Agreements? You will agree that there was no threat of force involved anymore, people were not under threat, people could go back home, couldn't they?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, Mr. Bakrac announced this question as a very important question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I get the feeling, but please correct me if I'm wrong, that Mr. Bakrac is moving in areas where your expertise might not allow you to give answers to all of his questions. If you feel that your expertise does not allow, don't hesitate to say because we are moving from demographic statistical analysis to an assessment of circumstances of matters which, as this Chamber and the Judges know and you most likely know as well, of an extremely complex nature what means force, what circumstances made it easy or less easy to move from one place to. If you look at the case law of this Tribunal, everyone will become aware of the complexity of this issue. So if you at any point feel that your expertise does not allow you to answer the questions with a sufficient level of reliability, do not hesitate to tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is what I was going to say, it was beyond my expertise to assess the circumstances. However, it was an interesting question for us to assess how many minority returns took place between 1995 December and the moment we provided our statistics for. Why? Because if there were many returns, so that only means that our statistics are far too low as a matter of fact, but and that is the my interest, of course, as demographer to understand what is the extent of the underestimation, which is, basically speaking, actually the conservative approach and underestimation is in favour of these defendants, of course. However, I must conclude that I studied minority returns, there are statistics published by UNHCR for the years after the war, and there were not that many minority return. There were returns but minorities were not returning in large numbers in these two years 1996 and 1997. So what I'm saying there is a certain degree of underestimation in our report of the displacement, especially internal displacement, but also external displacement, but, yeah, I think it is a good statistic simply to work with. They are conservative, they are methodologically solid based on good sources and can be documented with individual records, so that is all I have to say here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm looking at the clock, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm looking at the clock too. I'm looking at the clock too but I did have one question, Your Honour. Perhaps could we just have a minute or two because then we might round it off. Actually, we can do it after the break as well, but could Ms. Tabeau just explain to us how does this minimal return of refugees confirm her analysis. Let that be the question that will be answered after the break. Let us give the doctor a time to focus on it and say what she wishes to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much more time would you need apart from this question?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I assume that after the break I would need another half-hour and then I should be done. And I think that my colleague, Mr. Jordash, said that he will not take more than half an hour either. I don't think that he is actually hearing me now in a language he understands. Maybe things have changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, Mr. Bakrac was giving an assessment of how much time you would need. He thought that it might be half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think I need at least an hour, maybe an hour and 15 minutes. I did speak to Mr. Bakrac earlier, but we've changed our mind, I am afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's what he suggested as a possibility. We'll have a break and we'll resume at 6.00 and the parties are urged to confer and see whether there's any possibility to conclude the testimony of Ms. Tabeau today. If not, then we'll see how to proceed. We resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As always, the breaks are as busy, if not busier than court hearings and we apologise again for the late start. Mr. Bakrac, I think you asked the witness a question before the break. Perhaps she still remembers the question and could answer it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember. So minority returns, what is the impact of minority returns of the statistics of displaced persons and refugees presented in our IDP's and refugees report. Minority returns wouldn't be included as among the statistics, the numbers of displaced persons and refugees. Why? Because these persons would have be back home. So wouldn't be listed as displaced persons. So this is the source for an underestimation, what I'm saying is in fact there were more displaced persons, but because there were certain returns, not many, but there were returns, so the statistics that describe the status of displacement as of the fall of 1997, 1998, this is an underestimation of the actual number of displaced persons. And I have more reasons to believe that our numbers are an underestimation, the reasons are explained in the report in section 7. I'm not going to go into reasons but think for instance born after 1980 not included in our statistics, that is, children, think of unregistered voters, et cetera et cetera. These reasons, we tried to compensate for some of them by presenting the more complete estimate in our record. So et cetera et cetera, so our numbers are very conservative as a matter of fact, if you compare them with the UNHCR statistics, then you see that UNHCR is much less conservative.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, can we agree and can you agree with my view that your estimations are more of a mathematical nature and that to a lesser extent they indicate what the percentage of those who returned did so forcibly, of their own will or otherwise; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I didn't study the causes for displacement. It is just the statistics that describe the status of displacement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Dr. Tabeau. We were able to see the two primary sources that you drew upon. Do you know that following the Dayton Accords, in November 1995, some 30 to 40.000 Serbs who hailed from Sarajevo left Sarajevo. These were individuals who were on the census records in 1991 and that they were in fact the population that migrated to what later became these 11 municipalities. Were you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, I didn't study Sarajevo in our report. I did study the population of the voters as of 1997/1998, so newcomers were included in these statistics. So if there were any Serbs, from Sarajevo, who were listed in the census in 1991, and moved from Sarajevo and ended in any of these five municipalities or 11 split municipalities, they are included in statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The statistics, or rather, the voters' registers, did they show or did you draw any comparisons or try to find matches to establish whether a certain number of inhabitants who left Sarajevo were in fact later on on these voters' registers, or did you simply not try and identify if these persons are to be found on both these primary sources?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, it was so, the target population was the population who in 1991 lived, resided in the five municipalities. So for this target population, we traced them to see how they moved and whether they became displaced or not. So in displacement statistics, you will only see the population of the five municipalities and their movements. But there is a different, the second sort of statistics, this is the ethnic composition of municipalities. And the ethnic composition in 1991 is based on the census data, census population in five municipalities on one hand and on the other hand there is the ethnic composition of the population based on the voters' register 1997/1998. But still this is the population as reported in the voters' register, right, and matched with the census. So anybody who newcomer who moved into one of these municipalities and was reported in the census, would be listed as a newcomer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, if my understanding of what you are saying is correct, you now say that you focused on the population that was to be found in the the census record of 1991 in relation to these five municipalities; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: In displaced statistics, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes. Then in 1997/1998 there is a significant increase in Serb population in these five municipalities in terms of percentages. Can you explain to us the following: If you focused only on the population residing in these five municipalities according to the 1991 census, how did there come about a sharp increase in the number of Serbian inhabitants in these five municipalities?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: What I said I would repeat it. So for the ethnic composition we studied de facto population in 1991 versus 1997/1998, right? The 1997/1998 population was as reported in these municipalities, these municipalities meaning including also newcomers. Newcomers subject to being registered in the 1991 census. 1991 census in general in Bosnia-Herzegovina, right? Not necessarily in the five municipalities. There might have been municipalities from other municipality, of course there might have been newcomers from other municipalities. Were they from Sarajevo, I cannot say. I can check this and provide statistics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask to try to see if I understand, Mr. Bakrac, because I'm a bit surprised as a matter of fact by your question, rather than by the answer. If I have a population of 100.000, let's keep it simple, 50 per cent Serbs, 50 per cent Muslims. Yes. Now, if 49.000 of the Serbs -- of the Muslims leave, I'm not saying this is what happened, and let's say that all the Serbs remain, I'm not saying that this happened because usually the number in the statistics you see decreased slightly. Then from 50 per cent, suddenly you have close to 98 per cent Serbs. The shift in percentage, I'm trying to give you this answer to see -- to check also whether I understood it well, depends on how much Serbs are leaving, how many Muslims are leaving even if the Serbs were leaving in a certain number or their number decreased because they went elsewhere, but if the Muslims would have left in by far larger numbers, then the percentage of Serbs would of course increase. And now I do understand that Ms. Tabeau also is a bit cautious there because what -- how many Serbs there were in 1997 we do not exactly know because they might not all have registered as voters therefore also the percentages are limited to the matched persons which means that there may have been far -- at least a substantial number more of certain ethnicity but that they did not match and that they did not register as voters. Ms. Tabeau, I'm just trying to see whether I understand you well, and was again a bit surprised by the question of Mr. Bakrac because it seems relatively simple to me, but I might have underestimated the complexity -- one second, please. I might have underestimated the complexity, please tell me whether my understanding more or less matches your understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may, before the answer provide you with an explanation. It seems to me that Ms. Tabeau also raised her figures, not only estimates --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just first try to seek Ms. Tabeau's answer to my question whether I more or less understood --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Here is the thing, when preparing statistics on the displaced persons, we use the restriction that we only looked at the original 1991 population and for this population, only this population, from five municipalities we observed how many of them became displaced and how many just stayed in the original municipalities as they lived in 1991. That is one thing. So there was a restriction. However, if you assess changes in the ethnic composition, then it is de facto composition, de facto ethnic composition in 1991 and also 1997/1998. In five municipalities or 11 split municipalities. That means for the 1991, the population of the census is analysed and ethnic makeup of this population is shown. For 1997/8 it is all who registered in these municipalities for whom the ethnic makeup is shown. So there is no restriction here that the municipality of origin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, part of them might have come from another municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And at the same time it might be that there is another number which doesn't match at all which I ignored.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This doesn't mean I cannot make any other ethnic makeups, I can do all kind of makeups, this was the purpose to show the actual makeup as it became after the war versus as it used to be before the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And to the extent they had registered as voters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Bakrac, I'm glad that Ms. Tabeau at least corrected some of my understanding and it's important that the Chamber understands what the testimony is about. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'd rather I have an expert to guide me, but there we are, I'm trying to wade through the complex subject matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Madam Tabeau, to your knowledge, are voters registered used anywhere in the world for the development of scholarly demographic research?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is that a customary method?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: For the victims of war or regime, I would think it is not surprising that this source is used. For instance, for Cambodia, an American demographer, well established, known demographer, Patrick Heuveline used voters' register to estimate the number of victims of the Khmer Rouge regime. And it was a meaningful study that is respected and was published in a good scientific journal. The problem is that if you want to speak about sources on war victims, you can't keep in mind that these sources must be exactly the same as the sources on that in the peacetime. In the peacetime we had the official death notifications that are obligatorily to be made within three days from the moment a person dies. And there is a extended specific record of every death that is later processed in statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Therefore, Ms. Tabeau, if my understanding is correct and you'll correct me if I'm wrong, you say in such situation this method can be used, but do we agree that a voters' register is not an official basis for the development of a demographic study?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: It is not an official statistical source, that is not made by statistical authority, but you will be really surprised how many sources and what kind of sources are used in demographic studies, in historical demography, parish records, for instance, are often used, parish records that is the church records which are a very rich source of information about individuals, families, life histories of persons. I don't think that demography is restricted to standard sources like death notifications or -- in migration research, migration is a phenomenon, demographic phenomenon that is hard to document. We don't have in demography specific sources, systematic sources in which migration would be reported. Especially now in times of global movements of the population. Many people never register as migrants in the countries, yet this doesn't mean that they didn't change the place of residence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can data about ethnicity be found in these voters' registers?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: No, they don't include ethnicity, but ethnicity can be transferred from the census through the individual links of the voters' records, the census records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, there again the question surprises me because I think the report clearly explains what is the case, that is that you match personal details from persons in the voters' register with the 1991 census and since the 1991 census gives the ethnicity, that is the source of comparison, Ms. Tabeau, did I understand that well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. We always use the ethnicity as reported in the census.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clearly explained in her report. So that explanation would not be needed at all if there would be an ethnicity in the voters' register because that would have created a perhaps totally different picture. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, you said that when you took into account the data from 1991, you took into consideration the population born before 1980. Was it respect of 1991 everything taken into account which concerned individuals who were of age in that year including the individuals who were not of age in 1991, but could possibly be voters in the 1997 elections? Perhaps I should simplify, I take it by the expression on your face that I wasn't as precise that I should like have been. I'm not on the same expertise level as you are so I may even put a stupid question to you. What was the reason why the individuals born before 1980 were taken into consideration, let's start with that question and then we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: This is because of the second source that we use, the voters' register. We use two registers 1997/1998 but de facto, the vast majority of records in our register is from 1997. Actually, these two registers overlap greatly so there is a small number of records from 1998, we took all first registrations in 1997 as the core. So the voters' register represents the situation as of 1997. Now, in order to compare this population with the right population in 1991, one has to make a selection from the census in order to compare what is comparable and reject what is not comparable, so that is why the restriction on the year of birth.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So if my understanding is correct, you took into account in respect of 1991 those individuals which would in 1997 and 1998 have the legal age for voting; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. So the children were not taken for the analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, with the caveat that I tried to read your report as carefully as possible, I don't think found the following: Can you tell us what is the number of inhabitants who were 18 and above in 1991, what was the number of such inhabitants or percentage, and how many individuals did you take into account who were age 13, 14, 15 or 16 only because you knew that they would be eligible to vote in 1997 or 1998?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I think that I must explain to you that it is a longitudinal study that we did, right? So we work regarding voters, they are matched with the census. How can I explain this? I'm not sure I do understand your question correctly. So it's the restriction on age that make it is possible for me to extract a subgroup of the population in 1991, a subgroup in 1991, from which the voters originate. A large group of them becomes the voters, registered voters which I have in my source. So I'm still working with the same group of people. I'm extracting records from the census that all potentially will become the voters in 1997/1998 right. And in the census I take all of them, all potential voters, then I match them. Some are lost because they are not matched and that's it. This is how I make the statistic, I'm not sure I answered your question but that's the meaning of longitudinal and individual data, so the matching goes forth and back, it is still the same group, comparable group of individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So all the individuals whom you included in your calculations for these five municipalities were individuals who were on the population census records back in 1991 and bearing in mind all the aspects you referred to, you matched these individuals against the 1997 voters' register, including the category which was to become of age and eligible to vote in 1997 and 1998?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is the meaning, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, as for potential voters, did you also take into account the individuals who were back in 1991 aged 75 or above, or did you also have this upper age threshold in terms of the 1991 census?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: No, there was no upper age limit. So some probably died, some became war victims and died, but these numbers are not considerable especially not the number of deaths.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for my understanding, Ms. Tabeau, is it well understood that those of 75 year old in 1991 who had died before 1997 were just among the 20 per cent you could not match. They were just not there anymore.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably because they were not registered, they were not registered, they were not among the voters and they were not matched and rejected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was the registration of voters, was that done in 1997 itself, so it couldn't be that someone would register in 1995 as a voter -- no, no, we are talking about those who actually qualified in 1997, early 1998 as voters and had registered as such?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, so you did include a number of individuals who were on the 1991 census records as citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but had died a natural death by 1997/1998 and were not on the voters' register, so did you take such individuals into account and if so what is their percentage?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, I said that we didn't control for deaths, that means if somebody died, the person was not registered as a voter, it was not included in statistics. Who knows how many died during the war, there is no complete registration of natural deaths. There is a number of war deaths which is also uncertain but at least we have some ideas. So I could make a guesstimate, but I don't really want to speculate because the numbers we are talking about wouldn't have impacts on these statistics anyway. They wouldn't be shown as displaced persons anyway, that is simply not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, I'm nearing the end of my examination. Now, I have a couple of questions left. Kindly tell me if you included in your report the individuals who before the war went to work abroad and as you know, they were kept on the list of citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and who reported in 1997 having come back from abroad to vote in the elections, did you include them in your report and did you qualify them as refugees?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Actually, we studied this issue in detail, and there is one annex in the report in which the analysis is explained. If you could please refer to annex B4, B4, page 80 in the English version. So you see that we actually studied this issue thoroughly because those persons who left the country before the war, before the war, could create certain bias in our statistics. But obviously the number of such persons who could have introduced bias in our statistics is very small. As you will see in this annex there were about 28.000 of such persons who as a matter of fact didn't have a significant impact on the ethnic composition and not on the numbers of displaced persons and refugees. The error that is because of this small number is less than 5 per cent in the displacement statistics. So it is a fairly acceptable level of error in statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, let me conclude, with all due respect, your expertise is primarily that of a mathematical demographer; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In substance, your report and your study constitutes a statistical and mathematical overview of the size of the population without going into much detail into the reasons, the underlying reasons?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I said earlier today, I didn't study the causes for population displacement. It is just a measurement of the displacement that I studied.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Tabeau, I thank you and I apologise if my questions were not professional enough and if I taxed you in any way with my inexpert questions. Thank you, Your Honour, those were all the questions I had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Jordash, are you ready to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Jordash. Mr. Jordash is counsel for Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think just so that I'm clear, what we've established amongst a number of things is that your - I'm dealing with the first report, the IDP refugee report - your report doesn't deal with what happened between 1991 and 1997, it's just looking at what was the situation in 1991, what was the situation in 1997/1998?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me take you to your report, page 35, where you --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This is P1657.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You, in paragraph 2 make the comment that: "The 1992, 1995 conflict in Bosnia is an example of a humanitarian emergency in which a large civilian population was affected by war and cruel attempts to restructure the ethnic composition of the population, leading to large scale population displacement, deterioration of living conditions, severe health problems, and increased mortality." Now, I just want to pick up on some comments that you made in response to my learned friend Mr. Bakrac just before the break in which, forgive me if I'm wrong, but you appeared to suggest -- you appeared to go further than that and make comments concerning the non-accidental reasons for that displacement. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I didn't say -- I wouldn't say non-accidental, I would say I cannot agree that the usual causes of migration like educational migration, socio-economic migration, that includes work migration, we can say operated during the war period and caused these large numbers of the displacement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You wouldn't, would you, proffer an opinion concerning whether displacement was due to the war conditions generally as compared to, say, an ethnic group forcibly transferring another population out of a region?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: As I said, I didn't study the causes and I can only say I see the causes as most certainly different from usual and this is where my expertise ends with regard to causes of migration, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And "usual" is a reference to peacetime as compared to war time?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. Your opinion is that this is a displacement which is not usual in peacetime, it is characteristic of a war situation?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Most definitely not of a conflict -- not of a peace situation but of a war situation. If you think of the entire country Bosnia and Herzegovina, then it is about 50 per cent of the population who at the end of the war became displaced. We are speaking of 2.2 millions of people who were displaced. So that's the scale. It cannot be seen as regular migration, peacetime migration.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right. I don't think you and I are disagreeing about that. What I was looking at is whether you were trying to offer further opinion concerning whether these displacements that you record were the result of a specific activity during a war situation?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I don't think I was looking for such an explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: In my report, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Am I also correct in reading your report as not being able to cast comment on whether the displacement was the result of voluntary movement following the Dayton Agreement?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I didn't make any statements of this kind in the report. But what would be the voluntary movement following the Dayton Agreement, I wouldn't really know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Populations deciding they would rather live in the Federation rather than in the RS?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, I didn't comment on this in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But that was part of the Dayton Agreement, wasn't it? Certain areas designated to be governed by one ethnic group or religious group compared to other areas in the Federation?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I think it would be wrong to believe that all this migration took place after the Dayton Agreement. There are many documents, contextual documents, which I had opportunity to study, even though I didn't discuss them in the report which suggest that the migration was taking place in the war period.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, and I'm not suggesting all the movements did take place, but your report doesn't really comment on whether Dayton Agreement consequences or consequences during the war?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: No, I didn't look at this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, can I ask you to please turn to page 31 of P1657. I think just following on from what we've been discussing, looking at the statistics at the bottom of the page, in the period 1991 to 1997, the share of Serbs in the RS parts of Stanisic-Simatovic area increased from 52.5 to 92.5, i.e., by 76.4 per cent, and over the page, just looking at that paragraph and the next paragraph and I think you've given the statistics of -- I'm looking at the 95.3 per cent offered at the bottom of the page, the share of Muslims decreasing in the Serb -- RS part of the Stanisic-Simatovic area and over the page the share of Serbs decreasing in the Federation part by 99.3 per cent. Are there differences between those two figures statistically relevant?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Why would we compare these figures? I don't know, I didn't look at the significance of the differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You didn't?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I didn't, no. But this is not the point that to compare the differences, because I think the point is to measure what happened and express this in quantitative terms, this is why I didn't test the significance of the differences of the change.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can we have a look at page 25 then, please, just for some clarification for my understanding. Looking at Sanski Most on figure 10, could you just explain in straightforward terms what the figure 10 represents in relation to Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: It is the -- as the title says, the percentage of Serb displaced persons, both IDP's and refugees as of 1997/8 in relation to the entire population of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So does figure 10 suggest, I might be wrong about this I'm not --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: It's the number of 99.6 which is mentioned just above the figure, right, the dark part of the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So 80 to 100 per cent of the Serbs who were living in the Federation part of Sanski Most were displaced?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Exactly it is 99.6.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: That would be the interval you mentioned, 80 to 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, you also made the point that you considered that -- excuse me for paraphrasing, that overall movements of populations were occurring at the same time and likely to be parallel processes. Why do you reach that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Why do I reach this conclusion? Because I believe that the push factors, push factors were operating in the same time. Only that the direction of movement caused by the push factors was different for the Muslims and other non-Serbs and the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can I just have a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me just clarify, you're suggesting when you say parallel processes, parallel processes happening at some point between 1991 and 1997 or parallel processes which are actually happening at the same time, say for during particular incidents?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, first of all, let me clarify, I did not study the exact timing of the population movements because there is no data to study such a thing. So the data describes the status in 1991 and compares with 1997/1998. So what I can think of which is not surprising, it is just a straightforward thinking, is that certain factors were pushing out the population and forced them to move, all population, all ethnic groups. It is hard to imagine that these pushing factors were rapidly different at different moments of time, although it is not impossible, I would say, right? What I mean by parallel is the movements as such of the population, as measured using the data I had at my disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right. So your opinion in this regard -- well, let's stake Bosanski Samac -- sorry, let's take Sanski Most. It's the Prosecution case that in May of 1992 the Serbs attacked and took over Sanski Most. And so then moving forward in mid-1995, I think it's the Prosecution case that the Serbs were pushed out of Sanski Most, so your analysis of parallel processes would be in 1992, it's likely there was a transfer of non-Serb population out of Sanski Most, the parallel process is in 1995 the Serbs are pushed out of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: No, my thinking is not as you mentioned. My thinking is much simpler. I just measure what I can measure, and parallel for me means I clearly see that non-Serbs are moving out from Serb-controlled territories and Serbs are moving out from the federal territories. That would be the territories controlled by the federal government. Of course at different moments of times these controls were probably different over territories, but as I'm saying, I measure what I can measure and I don't discuss what I cannot measure. This is as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Are you aware of a refugee crisis arising from the Serbs being pushed out of Sanski Most in 1995?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The crisis meaning what?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Meaning --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: That they were living in large numbers, I mean, the Sanski Most FBiH-controlled territory, what do you mean by this crisis?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me show you an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: 65 ter 1D01635. It's a proposed exhibit, I guess. It's page 46 of the English and page 46 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And for your information, this is a diary or said to be a diary written by -- well, said by the Prosecution to be a diary written by Mladic, who obviously you must have heard of; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Obviously, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Page 46, which -- and just for your orientation the entry is dated the 22nd of September, 1995, and if we look at page --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I see the 25 of September -- of August, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We should be on, I hope, page 46 of the English at least. And bottom 5273. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And I hope that is matched by page 46 on the B/C/S. But just looking at the English, look at the bottom there: "By assessing the wave of refugees we can observe the change of mind after the 150.000 refugees from the RSK and the 120.000 refugees from Prijedor and Sanski Most ..." Did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, I'm reading this for the first time in my life, this particular paragraph, there is a mention of 120.000 refugees from Prijedor and Sanski Most and --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Have you seen things to corroborate that? Have you read documents in your studies which corroborate that number?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: First of all, I don't know what is the source for the number. This is one thing, how was it obtained, I have no idea. So I have right now no opinion about this particular number, how reliable it is, how close to reality it was. As I said, in my report, I did look at contextual sources, some of them are included in the report. Some are not but the statistics I prepared in the report are based on other sources and it is not so that every source will be 100 per cent consistent with another source, that's the whole thing about statistics on war victims, and displaced persons is just one type of war victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's put aside the exact number, these things are perhaps not close to the event exact science.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I am afraid not, you know, because if you look at the population size of Sanski Most Serbs and Prijedor, how one could come to 120.000 Serb refugees from these two municipalities only?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I guess it would depend on who was living there at the time?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: We have the census to check how many lived there at the moment of the census.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: At the moment of 1995 we don't have a census, do we?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: No, we don't, that's correct except for the Banja Luka census and Sanski Most is part of it. So is Prijedor and I still don't think this 120.000 is consistent with that statistic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Have you read contextual sources which do cast a light on the refugee crisis which this seems to be referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly pause between questions and answers, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what contextual sources. You gave me one example, I said, no, I'm unaware with this one example you gave me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm asking you to consider from your broad experience, the wide range of material you must have read over the years, whether you have heard at all about the refugees which fled from the attacks in September of 1995 in Sanski Most? If you haven't, then that's fine.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, yes, this is what I wanted to say. I did not study this particular episode of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: So I did study sources, but not particularly related to this particular episode.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So you can't provide any assistance in what the situation might have been?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Based on my report?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, no, based on your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Not immediately, I couldn't. No. Not immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You would be able to though if we were to come back, or if you were to come back?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I don't know. I would start a search and see what I could find. But the problem is that finding is one thing and assessing is another. I am afraid assessing of -- assessment of sources is an important issue, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Well, for now, nothing --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I would need more time than just one day or something to bring assessments, say. Sources plus assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: For now, nothing then comes to mind.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Not immediately, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I notice the time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We have to consider how to proceed tomorrow. I'm thinking about, of course, the next witness waiting. I'm sorry, Ms. Tabeau, we are talking about the next witness, but for scheduling purpose we cannot avoid that. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The next witness is in The Hague and is ready to appear tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ready to appear. Of course we are thinking about whether that witness can be concluded, Ms. Tabeau, perhaps I simply explain to you, that whether or not we'll continue to hear your evidence or whether we would prefer to start with another witness who has to travel and which we would very much like to conclude this week is a matter still under consideration. How much time you would need for the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have the witness scheduled for three hours. I think I've' taken every reasonable measure to try to reduce that time with a number of mechanisms. I hope to be substantially less than that, but I'm really reluctant to give an estimate other than to say I think I will be substantially less than the three hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So which brings some two hours in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On my mind, not yet on the clock. Yes. Could I hear from the other Defence teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It is very difficult to assess, as Mr. Groome has said he has taken many measures but those measures necessarily put work on us. So we've been served yesterday with a 22-page exhibit chart with detailed comments upon it which we haven't even had the chance to go through. The witness I think is going to make some various comments about intercepts which we are not precisely sure of at this stage. And so it's -- I wouldn't like to say less than three hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with every possible reservation my best guess would be three hours as well. Perhaps it's going to be shorter than that, but perhaps we'll even have to ask you for some more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What about using Friday morning instead of a housekeeping session?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think I would prefer that to a housekeeping session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you would prefer that. Yes. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Likewise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do therefore see that you both are available Friday morning, is that the right conclusion? We'll seriously consider that also in view of the witnesses we'll have to travel back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Keeping in the back of our mind that we might keep the Friday morning and we have a day scheduled for a housekeeping session early next week, that leads the Chamber to give us guidance to the parties that we like to conclude the testimony of Ms. Tabeau tomorrow and Mr. Jordash time needed for that? May I urge you to ask Ms. Tabeau about what is in her report and not to spend 70 per cent of your time on identifying what is not in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Point taken, Your Honour. I think no more than 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which brings you well over the estimate of one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, I don't want to take up too much time. If I could say 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- if you could conclude your cross-examination in 30 minutes. Mr. Farr, how much time do you think you would need to re-examination? For you the same is true, let's ask what we cannot read in the report and not what either we can read in the report or what doesn't appear in the report because if it isn't there then it's not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: It would be just a few minutes, Your Honour, if anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Few minutes. That's taken. Then we would like to see you back tomorrow at quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon, Ms. Tabeau. I would like to instruct you that you should not speak nor communicate in any other way with anyone about your testimony either given today or given tomorrow and there's a fair chance that we would conclude hearing your evidence in a little bit over half an hour. We stand adjourned and we'll resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 8th of December at quarter past 2.00 in this same courtroom.
